"But in the case of Obama, he does represent hope, not only for the States but for the whole world." For Obama look-alike actor Lamar, there was some irony about getting flown to Turkey to star in a commercial for a bank. He is a recent casualty of the global economic crisis. "I was laid off in January of this year from JP Morgan Chase Bank in the U.S.," Lamar said, in a telephone interview from Pennsylvania. "After 18 years in the company, I was just laid off. One of the cutbacks. I'm currently unemployed right now." Or, was unemployed. Lamar's striking resemblance to the American president has suddenly offered the former software analyst a possible new career for supporting his wife and child. "I'm available full-time now," Lamar said. "I'm going to see where this leads me." Lamar is now being represented by a casting agency in Los Angeles that specializes in celebrity look-alikes. Since he discovered his new "talent," he has traveled to the Netherlands to appear in a commercial for a liquor chain and to Paris, where an activist organization brought him in to meet lawmakers at the National Assembly, as part of a campaign to raise awareness about racism and racial profiling in France. "This was very exciting for me, a true privilege!" Lamar said. During his brief visit to Turkey, locals did double-takes when they saw Lamar walk past. "Even in the studio, the crew [members] were like, 'Oh! Is that Obama?" said Celikbilek of Alametifarika advertising. Using the image of an American president to promote anything in Turkey is a remarkable reversal. U.S. approval ratings in Turkey plunged to 9 percent, according to a 2007 Pew Research poll, making America less popular in Turkey then almost anywhere else in the world, even though the two countries are NATO allies. There was widespread anger among Turks at the war in neighboring Iraq. But the election of Barack Obama appears to have dramatically improved perceptions of America. "Bush was a dictator who attacked other countries," said Abdurrahman Ozdemir, who sells cigarettes from a small stall on the street. "But we love Obama ... because he does not want to go to war with other countries." "We started to love and like America because of Obama," said a 33-year-old woman named Begum Arinc. "I don't want to see people dying. I don't want to see any war. That's why I want to believe in Obama."

The speaker is Michael Lamar, who lost his job in January and has since found work impersonating Barack Obama.

“I wish I could announce an economic package like this,” he says. “But a Turkish bank has already done so. It is Garanti. I wish Garanti existed in America.”

Despite appearances, the segment is not a real presidential announcement. It is a Turkish television advertisement featuring Lamar, a 44-year-old Obama look-alike from Whitehall, Pennsylvania, promoting a bank in Turkey.

During the month leading up to the actual President Obama’s visit to Turkey, the campaign appeared nationwide on TV and billboards. It used the U.S. president’s recognizable, Warhol-style image to market loans with low interest rates.

The advertising executives who developed the idea said Lamar was ideally suited to promote what they called Garanti Bank’s version of an economic stimulus plan.

“We probably would not have made this advertisement with the former president,” said Can Celikbilek, a copywriter at the advertising agency Alametifarika. “Obama, however, symbolizes hope—not only for the United States, but for the entire world.”

There is a certain irony in Lamar being flown to Turkey to appear in a bank commercial: he recently became one of the victims of the worldwide economic downturn.

“I was laid off from JP Morgan Chase Bank in the United States in January of this year,” Lamar said during a phone interview from Pennsylvania. “After spending 18 years with the company, I was simply let go as part of the cutbacks. At the moment, I’m unemployed.”

Or at least he was. Lamar’s remarkable similarity to the American president has unexpectedly created the possibility of a new profession, one that could help him provide for his wife and child.

“I’m free to do this full-time now,” he said. “I’m going to find out where it takes me.”

A Los Angeles casting company specializing in celebrity doubles now represents Lamar. Since recognizing this newfound “talent,” he has gone to the Netherlands to film an advertisement for a chain of liquor stores. He has also traveled to Paris, where an activist group arranged for him to meet legislators at the National Assembly as part of an effort to draw attention to racism and racial profiling in France.

“It was extremely exciting and a genuine privilege,” Lamar said.

While making his short trip to Turkey, Lamar prompted surprised second looks from people who saw him passing by.

“Even members of the studio crew reacted by saying, ‘Oh! Is that Obama?’” recalled Celikbilek of Alametifarika.

The idea of using an American president’s likeness to sell anything in Turkey represents an extraordinary change. According to a Pew Research survey conducted in 2007, approval of the United States among Turks had fallen to 9 percent. That made America less popular in Turkey than in nearly any other country, despite Turkey and the United States being NATO partners.

Much of the hostility stemmed from broad public outrage in Turkey over the war in neighboring Iraq. Barack Obama’s election, however, seems to have significantly changed Turkish attitudes toward the United States.

“Bush was a dictator who invaded other nations,” said Abdurrahman Ozdemir, a cigarette vendor operating from a small roadside stand. “But we love Obama because he does not want to wage war against other countries.”

Begum Arinc, a 33-year-old woman, expressed a similar view.

“Obama has made us begin to like and love America,” she said. “I don’t want people to die, and I don’t want any wars. That is why I want to put my faith in Obama.”

**New York (CNN)** — When former bank employee Michael Lamar lost his job, he did not expect his resemblance to President Barack Obama to launch a new career — or land him in a television commercial halfway around the world.

But Lamar’s familiar smile, close-cropped hair and presidential profile caught the attention of advertisers seeking an Obama look-alike for a campaign by Turkey’s Garanti Bank.

In the commercial, Lamar channels the confidence and mannerisms associated with the 44th U.S. president, whose “Yes, we can” message became internationally recognized during the 2008 campaign. The advertisement uses that resemblance to give the Turkish bank’s promotion a timely political twist.

For Lamar, the role marked a dramatic change after unemployment. The former banking worker went from looking for a paycheck to appearing on television as a stand-in for one of the world’s most recognizable figures.

The part also required more than simply looking like Obama. Lamar studied the president’s measured speaking style, gestures and posture to make the performance convincing.

The commercial is another example of Obama’s global cultural reach following his historic election as the first Black president of the United States. His image and campaign themes quickly appeared in advertising, entertainment and popular culture far beyond American borders.

Lamar is not the president, and the commercial did not feature or carry an endorsement from Obama. But for an unemployed former bank employee with a striking resemblance, the role offered an unexpected opportunity — and proof that sometimes a familiar face can open doors.

**Obama Double Takes Center Stage in Turkish Loan Commercial**

**ISTANBUL —** Days before U.S. President Barack Obama was due to arrive in Turkey, Turkish television viewers were introduced to another “Obama” — this one offering low-interest consumer loans.

Michael Lamar, an American actor and Obama look-alike, appears in a new commercial designed to capitalize on the excitement surrounding the president’s visit. Dressed in a dark suit and wearing Obama’s familiar close-cropped hairstyle, Lamar recreates the president’s measured gestures, confident stride and campaign-style presence as the advertisement promotes affordable credit to Turkish consumers.

The commercial carefully avoids saying that the man on screen is Obama. But the resemblance, staging and timing leave little doubt about the intended association. Its message echoes the optimism of Obama’s 2008 presidential campaign, applying the language of hope and possibility to a far more immediate concern for many Turkish households: obtaining a loan at a manageable interest rate.

The advertisement began attracting attention on Turkish television and online as the country prepared for Obama’s visit in early April 2009. Obama was scheduled to hold talks with Turkish leaders in Ankara, address parliament and travel to Istanbul for meetings connected with the Alliance of Civilizations initiative.

His decision to include Turkey in his first major European trip as president was widely interpreted as an effort to repair relations with the Muslim world and underline Turkey’s importance as a NATO ally, regional power and bridge between Europe and the Middle East.

Advertisers, meanwhile, saw a rare cultural moment.

Lamar’s performance relies less on dialogue than on instantly recognizable mannerisms: the deliberate pauses, slight lift of the chin and open-handed gestures associated with Obama’s public appearances. The production uses presidential-looking lighting and camera angles while stopping short of reproducing official U.S. symbols.

That distinction is important. Obama did not endorse the loan campaign, and there is no suggestion that the White House approved or participated in the commercial. The actor is presented as a parody or impersonation rather than as the president himself.

The campaign arrives during a difficult economic period. Turkey, like much of the world, was feeling the effects of the global financial crisis, with slowing growth, tighter credit and rising anxiety about jobs and household finances. Against that background, low-interest personal loans had become an especially competitive area for Turkish banks and finance companies.

By borrowing Obama’s image, the commercial seeks to give a routine financial product a sense of novelty and momentum. The approach also reflects the extraordinary visibility Obama enjoyed in Turkey after his election as the first Black president of the United States.

His popularity did not erase long-standing tensions in Turkish-American relations. Public opinion in Turkey had deteriorated sharply during the presidency of George W. Bush, particularly after the 2003 invasion of Iraq. Turkish officials were also closely watching Obama’s position on several sensitive issues, including Iraq, relations with Armenia and Washington’s approach to the broader Middle East.

Even so, anticipation surrounding the visit was evident across Istanbul. Newspapers devoted extensive coverage to Obama’s itinerary and security preparations. Television channels aired profiles of the president and discussions of what his trip might mean for bilateral relations. Souvenir sellers and marketers quickly incorporated his name and image into products and promotions.

Lamar’s appearance placed the loan advertisement among the most conspicuous examples of that commercial enthusiasm.

Obama impersonators had already become sought-after performers in the United States after the 2008 campaign, appearing at private events, corporate gatherings and on television. In Turkey, however, Lamar’s role carried an additional layer of symbolism. The real president was arriving with promises of renewed dialogue; his double was already on screen promising easier access to credit.

The advertisement drew amusement from many viewers, though it also prompted questions about the use of a sitting foreign leader’s likeness to sell financial services. Such campaigns often occupy a legal and ethical gray area, depending on whether they are considered parody, imitation or misleading endorsement.

In this case, the commercial’s exaggerated presentation and the use of a professional look-alike make the joke apparent. Still, its success depends entirely on viewers recognizing Obama and transferring some of the excitement surrounding him to the advertised loans.

For Lamar, the role demonstrates the international reach of the Obama phenomenon. For the advertiser, it offers a way to stand out in Turkey’s crowded banking market. And for Turkish audiences awaiting the U.S. president’s arrival, it provides an unusual preview: an Obama-like figure speaking not about diplomacy, NATO or peace in the Middle East, but about interest rates.

By the time the real president reached Turkey, his look-alike had already made the case that the spirit of “Yes, we can” could be applied to borrowing money as easily as to winning elections.

Michael Lamar never planned on becoming “Barack Obama.” For years, the Pennsylvania man had a conventional career as a software analyst at JPMorgan Chase. But after losing that job, Lamar—then 44—had to look for a new way to earn a living.

Friends and strangers had long remarked on his resemblance to President Obama: the lean face, close-cropped hair and broad smile. With his technology career interrupted, Lamar decided to turn that resemblance into a profession. He studied Obama’s measured speaking rhythm, pauses, gestures and presidential wave, added a dark suit and flag pin, and began marketing himself as a look-alike.

The most promising demand came from overseas, particularly in China, where Obama was instantly recognizable and an American impersonator was a novelty. Lamar was hired for corporate appearances, promotional events, photographs and entertainment programs. He generally did not need to deliver long political speeches; much of the act depended on entering a room with presidential confidence, greeting people in Obama’s cadence and posing for crowds eager to take pictures.

The career was an unlikely reversal. Losing a stable banking job had left Lamar uncertain about his future, but it also pushed him to capitalize on something he had previously treated as a joke. Overseas, his resemblance became a marketable skill and gave him a second career—one built less on software than on performance, timing and the global celebrity of America’s first Black president.

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a journalistic piece examining the irony and political significance of a laid-off American bank worker portraying President Obama in Garanti Bank’s Turkish “economic stimulus” advertising campaign.

### Obama’s Double, and the Strange Journey of the Stimulus

At first glance, Garanti Bank’s Turkish advertising campaign offers a familiar image of political reassurance: Barack Obama, or someone who looks remarkably like him, promising economic relief with the confidence of a president confronting a crisis.

But the man in the commercial is not Obama. He is an American bank worker who lost his job amid the financial turmoil. Now, made up and costumed as the president, he is helping a Turkish bank sell its own version of an “economic stimulus.”

The casting turns an otherwise playful advertisement into a compact parable of the global financial crisis. A worker displaced by the American banking system has found employment impersonating the politician charged with rescuing that system. His likeness is then used abroad by another bank to borrow the language—and some of the authority—of Washington’s response.

The result is comic, but the joke rests on a serious inversion. Obama’s stimulus was designed to revive demand, stabilize employment and prevent a deep recession from becoming a depression. In Garanti’s hands, “stimulus” becomes a marketing device: less a program of public spending than an invitation to consumers to borrow, spend or take advantage of favorable banking terms.

That translation from public policy into commercial branding says much about Obama’s early international image. Soon after his election, he was not merely an American president but a global symbol of action, optimism and institutional competence. His face could communicate recovery even where the details of his administration’s policies were remote or poorly understood. Garanti did not need the real president’s endorsement. It needed the emotional shorthand attached to him.

The impersonator’s biography complicates that optimism. The financial crisis was often described in abstractions—frozen credit markets, toxic assets, recapitalization—but its consequences were borne by employees who had little influence over the decisions that produced it. Here, one of those workers re-enters the economy by performing confidence on behalf of a bank.

That is the advertisement’s sharpest irony: the laid-off worker becomes employable by resembling the most powerful man responding to his unemployment.

In Turkey, the campaign also carried political significance. Turkish banks and officials were eager to distinguish the country’s financial system from the badly damaged institutions of the United States and Western Europe. Yet the commercial demonstrates how strongly American political imagery continued to shape the global vocabulary of economic leadership. Even a Turkish bank presenting its own remedy reached for the face of an American president.

The advertisement therefore works on two levels. It localizes a global crisis, suggesting that Garanti can deliver its own consumer-scale rescue. At the same time, it domesticates Obama, turning a distant head of state into an approachable salesman. The authority of government is borrowed to legitimize a private offer, while the trauma of unemployment is converted into entertainment.

There is no evidence in the performance of presidential power itself—only its visual reproduction. That distinction matters. The real stimulus involved legislative battles, public debt and arguments over the proper role of the state. The commercial version compresses those disputes into a recognizable suit, voice and smile.

For Garanti, the device was clever advertising. For viewers, it was an easily understood joke. But beneath the humor lay an uncomfortable portrait of the post-crisis economy: governments rescuing banks, banks selling recovery, and workers adapting however they could—even if that meant putting on the face of the man expected to save them.
